name: Black String
description: Schwarzschild's black hole extended along one more direction of space, a static vacuum solution of gravity in five or more dimensions whose horizon is a cylinder. Ruth Gregory and Raymond Laflamme showed in 1993 that ripples along it longer than about seven horizon radii grow, and numerical evolutions of that instability end in a naked singularity.
convention: The horizon radius is fixed by the string's mass per unit length, $M/L$. We keep factors of $c$ explicit.
history: Take Schwarzschild's black hole and hand space one more direction, $z$, along which nothing changes [gregory2012]. The curvature has no components along $z$, so the result solves the vacuum Einstein equations in five dimensions with no further work [gregory2012]. Its line element is $$ds^2 = -\left(1 - \frac{r_s}{r}\right)c^2dt^2 + \left(1 - \frac{r_s}{r}\right)^{-1}dr^2 + r^2d\Omega^2 + dz^2,$$ and its horizon is a cylinder, a sphere of radius $r_s$ at every $z$: a black string, which needs at least five dimensions to live in [gregory2012]. String theory has ten to offer, and in its low energy limit Gary Horowitz and Andrew Strominger found in 1991 "a variety of solutions with the structure of an extended object surrounded by an event horizon" [horowitz1991]. Wrap $z$ into a circle, the fifth dimension of Kaluza and Klein, and from four dimensions the string "looks just like a Schwarzschild black hole" [gregory2012].¶Is it stable? Ruth Gregory and Raymond Laflamme asked in 1988, looked for a growing mode, found none, and reported that the string "is stable against linearized perturbations of the metric" [gregory1988, gregorylaflamme1993]. Yet a long string has less entropy than it could have [gregorylaflamme1993]. A length $L$ of string with mass $M$ has an entropy proportional to $M^2/L$, and one round black hole of five dimensions with the same mass has an entropy proportional to $M^{3/2}$, so for a long enough piece the round hole has more [gregorylaflamme1993]. In 1993 they put the initial data on a surface that ends on the future horizon, clear of the neck of Schwarzschild's wormhole, and found a mode that grows as $e^{\Omega t}$ [gregorylaflamme1993].¶The mode that grows is a ripple along the string, the Gregory-Laflamme instability: the horizon swells at some values of $z$ and thins at others, as $\cos kz$ [gregory1994]. Only long ripples grow, those with $kr_s < 0.876$, a wavelength of more than about $7.2\,r_s$ [gubser2002, lehner2010]. That is a little more than the horizon's circumference, $2\pi r_s$, and you have watched its cousin at the kitchen tap, where a thin stream of water breaks into drops [cardoso2006, eggers1997]. A cylinder of liquid "longer than its circumference is energetically unstable to breakup", a result of Joseph Plateau's for which Lord Rayleigh computed the growth rate [cardoso2006]. Treat the horizon as a membrane with surface tension and the two thresholds nearly coincide: Vitor Cardoso and Óscar Dias found "good agreement for the threshold mode in all dimensions" in 2006 [cardoso2006]. On a circle shorter than the critical wavelength the ripple does not fit and the string is stable, so the small extra dimensions of string theory leave astrophysical black holes alone [gregorylaflamme1993].¶What does an unstable string turn into? Gregory and Laflamme suggested that it fragments into round black holes, and a horizon can split only at a naked singularity, which Roger Penrose's cosmic censorship hypothesis rules out [gregorylaflamme1993, penrose1969]. The horizon "cannot pinch off in finite time", Gary Horowitz and Kengo Maeda proved in 2001, the time being the affine parameter along the horizon's generators, and they expected the string to settle into a new static shape, lumpy along $z$ [horowitz2001]. Lumpy strings do exist: Steven Gubser built them in perturbation theory and Toby Wiseman on a computer, with the horizon up to nine times wider at its bulge than at its waist [gubser2002, wiseman2003]. For a circle of given length they are heavier than the uniform string, so "they cannot be the end state of the instability" [wiseman2003].¶The answer came from evolving the string on a computer: the first attempt, by Matthew Choptuik and five collaborators in 2003, saw it head toward "a sequence of spherical black holes connected by thin black strings" before the code failed [choptuik2003]. With a new code in 2010, Luis Lehner and Frans Pretorius found a cascade: each thin segment is itself a black string longer than its own critical wavelength, so it beads up in turn, into "ever-smaller satellite black holes" joined by "ever-thinner string segments" [lehner2010]. Each generation takes about a quarter of the time of the one before, so the times add up to a finite total, and the segments reach zero radius about $115\,r_s/c$ after the start [lehner2010]. A distant observer sees the curvature diverge in a finite time with no fine tuning of the initial data, "a generic violation of cosmic censorship" [lehner2010]. Horowitz and Maeda's theorem stands all the same: Donald Marolf had noted in 2005 that an infinite affine parameter along the horizon can be "a finite advanced time" for an observer far away [marolf2005].¶Is the string a special case? A black hole spinning fast enough in six or more dimensions spreads into a pancake, and Roberto Emparan and Robert Myers argued in 2003 that near its centre the pancake is a black membrane, unstable as the string is [emparan2003]. A thin black ring in five dimensions resembles a boosted black string, and when Pau Figueras, Markus Kunesch, and Saran Tunyasuvunakool evolved one in 2016 its horizon grew "bulges connected by necks which become ever thinner over time" [figueras2016]. A ring needs no dimension rolled into a circle, and they called the result "the first concrete evidence" that cosmic censorship can fail in an asymptotically flat spacetime of five dimensions [figueras2016]. For the string itself, Figueras, Tiago França, Chenxia Gu, and Tomas Andrade repeated the evolution in 2023 for strings of different lengths and confirmed "the pinch off of the horizon in finite asymptotic time", with no single ratio between the times of successive generations [figueras2023].

related.text: The black string is Schwarzschild's black hole at every point of a line. Every slice of constant $z$ is Schwarzschild's spacetime [gregory2012].

The other way to carry Schwarzschild's black hole into five dimensions, with a round horizon, a 3-sphere. It has more entropy than a long enough piece of string of the same mass [gregorylaflamme1993].

Another vacuum solution of five dimensions with one direction rolled into a circle. Seen from four dimensions the string is Schwarzschild's black hole and the monopole is a magnetic charge [gregory2012, grossperry1983].
A wall in anti-de Sitter space of five dimensions, on which Schwarzschild's black hole is a black string that reaches away from the wall into the fifth [chamblin2000].
The black string with its extra direction a circle, set moving around it. Seen from four dimensions the moving string is an electrically charged black hole [horowitz2012].
A black ring in orbit around a black hole. Where the ring is thin it is a black string bent into a circle, and it is expected to ripple as the string does [elvang2006, elvang2007].
The extreme member of Horowitz and Strominger's charged black three-branes, a sheet of three dimensions with a horizon and no singularity behind it [horowitz1991, gibbons1995].

The black string with a magnetic field through its spheres and a second radius $r_B$, where the circle shrinks to a point. Put $r_B$ outside the horizon and the horizon is gone: the string has become a star whose space ends on a bubble [bah2021].

Another family that branches off where an instability sets in: spinning black holes with a cloud of scalar field branch off Kerr's at the threshold of superradiance, and Herdeiro and Radu set them beside the rippled strings of the Gregory-Laflamme instability [herdeiro2014].

coordinates.name: Schwarzschild

parameters.description: Schwarzschild radius, $r_s = 2GM/(c^2L)$ for a length $L$ of string of mass $M$, with $G$ Newton's constant in five dimensions

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi, z)$, Schwarzschild's with the length $z$ along the string added, and $t$ carrying dimensions of time. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Ingoing Eddington-Finkelstein

parameters.description: Schwarzschild radius, $r_s = 2GM/(c^2L)$ for a length $L$ of string of mass $M$, with $G$ Newton's constant in five dimensions

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(v, r, \theta, \phi, z)$, with the advanced time $v = ct + r + r_s\ln\left|r/r_s - 1\right|$ a length and $z$ the length along the string.

coordinates.name: Kerr-Schild

parameters.description: Schwarzschild radius, $r_s = 2GM/(c^2L)$ for a length $L$ of string of mass $M$, with $G$ Newton's constant in five dimensions

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(T, r, \theta, \phi, z)$, with the time $T = (v - r)/c = t + (r_s/c)\ln\left|r/r_s - 1\right|$ of the ingoing Eddington-Finkelstein chart carrying dimensions of time and $z$ the length along the string. We take components in the chart $x^0 = cT$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{T}$ means $d(cT)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Schwarzschild, Six Dimensions

parameters.description: Horizon radius, $r_h^2 = 8GM/(3\pi c^2L)$ for a length $L$ of string of mass $M$, with $G$ Newton's constant in six dimensions

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \psi, \theta, \phi, z)$ in $D = 6$, the static chart of the Schwarzschild-Tangherlini black hole of five dimensions with the length $z$ along the string added, and $t$ carrying dimensions of time. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
